_doc: AUTHORED CONTENT — the Director-approved research corpus (finalization proposal v2, 2026-10-01; ADR-029 addendum A, ADR-030). It started as the ADR-029 migration of tech-graph-v0.6.json (read-only) and was then curated; nothing regenerates it. scripts/research-content-audit.py writes the audit from it.
key: the STABLE integer id carried by save rows and orders. Never renumber a key; append new nodes with new keys.
prereq / researchStage.requires / eurekas[].when / entities[].requires: D-020 predicate dialect with AND/OR/NOT keywords and boolean atoms (ADR-029 §11).
cost: content-derived, BaseCost = U × K^magnitude (tuning.costModel); costRationale carries the six factors per node. Calibration adjustments: none. Never depth-derived (ADR-029 R-10 is overridden).
tuning.rpPerTurn: Research Points per strategic turn, never multiplied by dt (ADR-030). Coefficient and exponent are calibration values.
eurekas[].weight: the fraction of BaseCost the condition credits once; a node's weights sum to at most tuning.accelerationCreditCeilingFraction. Eureka and foreign exposure share that one pool.
baseline: capabilities a founded civilization has with zero completed nodes (D-045 §1) — outside the graph; ownership contract in docs/design/research-capability-ownership.md.

sectorActivities: the five labour sectors (code, kernel-contract surface) and the ACTIVITY each one expresses (ADR-033 D1). Every sector is baseline and never gated; its turn-1 identity is a baseline identity (providedBy names baseline entries), and a researched identity (an activity entity) REPLACES it or JOINS it once the entity is knowledge-eligible. Presentation only: production, yields and shares are unchanged. label overrides the entity's name for the sector (herding also fishes).

source.generator: authored — Director finalization proposal v2 (final), curated from the ADR-029 migration

rpPerTurn.input: population (military population weighted below 1 — weight is a calibration parameter, inert until soldier accounting exists)
rpPerTurn.unit: Research Points per strategic turn — scoped exception to law 3 (ADR-030); never multiplied by dt

costModel.U_basis: unit calibration: a magnitude-0 node takes a founded civilization (5,000 people, 30.8 RP/turn) 3 turns
costModel.K_basis: content scale: each magnitude point doubles cognitive effort
costModel.magnitude: novelty + difficulty + material + institutional + breadth + prerequisite complexity; Age enters only as a bounded prior inside difficulty and institutional

tuning._cityStatePaceFraction: R2a (docs/city-state-progression.md; Director decisions 4 and 12). TUNE, CHOSEN (L6): an UNCONTROLLED settlement researches autonomously with RP = cityStatePaceFraction x rpPerTurn(its own population). Reference: Civ VI city-states do not research at all; the Director rules ours progress slowly. 0.25 of the organized rate (before the sublinearity penalty of being one settlement) keeps a city-state substantially slower than a civilization of the same population. 0 disables city-state research.

civicsPoints.unit: Civics Points per sim-year, integrated over dtYears (law 3) and banked in integer milli-CP: generated per step = floor(1000 x coefficientPerYear x population^exponent x dtYears); a city-state's is x cityStatePaceFraction

tuning._civicsPoints: ADR-043 (D-062, the Director's 2026-10-22 ruling): Civics Points fund ONLY the Civics target; Research Points fund ONLY the Technology target. CP is banked without cap or loss (Balance = Generated - Spent). Population is the same input RP reads; the PROPOSED coefficient 0.008/yr equals RP's 0.08/turn at a 10-year turn. enabled false restores the v34 one-pool model (civics funded by RP, one target) — the attribution switch. Other CP sources (institutions, specialists, embassies, spies, artists, scholars) and the RP<->CP exchange are DEFERRED.

baseline.name: Settlement founding
baseline.providedBy: ColonizationSystem — a colony is founded when famine-flight migrants have no viable settlement to move to (MigrationSystem demand), or by a Found Settlement order (OrderKind 9, D-051 §5, ADR-036) from a settlement the issuer controls to an unclaimed, reachable site; founding is instantaneous — no settler unit exists

baseline.name: Scouting and exploration
baseline.providedBy: not yet simulated — no mobile agents exist (D-043)

baseline.name: Basic military (clubmen or equivalent)
baseline.providedBy: not yet simulated — the battle layer is a later milestone (D-011)

baseline.name: Basic food and resource gathering
baseline.providedBy: ProductionSystem — the Farming, Herding/fishing and Extraction sectors produce food and goods with no research (HarvestWeatherSystem supplies only the harvest multiplier); no sector is gated: research changes the ACTIVITY a sector expresses (activity.farming, .herding, .logging, .mining; sectorActivities) (ADR-033 D1); one exception changes output: with farming.preCultivation on (sim.json), the Farming sector harvests wild food at the forager rates until activity.farming is eligible for the settlement, and the cultivated yield applies once it is (R2a)

baseline.name: Basic internal construction
baseline.providedBy: ConstructionSystem — an EnqueueConstruction order queues a project; the first project in a settlement's queue is built a little each turn, as far as its materials and builders allow, and is complete when all its materials and work have gone in (what has gone in is kept while it waits and lost only if it is cancelled; D-054); no Builder unit

baseline.name: Migration and resettlement
baseline.providedBy: MigrationSystem — people move between settlements with no research

baseline.name: Fire: making, keeping and cooking
baseline.providedBy: not separately simulated — fire is known before the simulation begins (D-047 ruling 2); no node gates it, and fire_making is advanced controlled-fire use

baseline.name: Primitive tools and simple hafting
baseline.providedBy: not separately simulated — the tools good comes from crafting recipes that read no research; simple hafting and binding need no node (D-047 ruling 3), composite hafting is technology-owned

baseline.name: Basic fishing (shore, net, trap and spear)
baseline.providedBy: ProductionSystem — the Herding/fishing sector produces food from turn 1 with no research; activity.fishing requires no node (D-047 rulings 4-6), fish weirs and line/pelagic fishing are technology-owned

baseline.name: Primitive riverine and shore-hugging craft
baseline.providedBy: not yet simulated as vessels — no vessel, port or sea route exists; river movement is priced from founding by the TraversalLattice river-corridor coefficient, which reads no research (D-047 ruling 7)

baseline.name: Basic shelter
baseline.providedBy: HousingSystem — dwellings are endowed at founding and built and maintained with no research and no order

baseline.name: Basic paths and overland movement
baseline.providedBy: PathBuildSystem — dirt paths (the DirtPath edge type) accrue from use with no research and no order (D-047 ruling 8)

baseline.name: Hunting
baseline.providedBy: ProductionSystem — SIMULATED as the Herding/fishing sector's yield from wild-animal (livestock) deposits: the sector's labour turns each settlement's livestock deposit into livestock with no research. No separate hunting sector, prey population or hunting mechanism exists (the Director lists hunting as baseline, integration directive 2026-10-02; ADR-033 D1)

researchStage.requires: medicine_hippocratic AND (geometry_axiomatic OR algebra) AND stamp_seal
researchStage._doc: Knowledge-level reading of the university / research institutional stage (D-044 R4): building.university's technology requirement AND building.library's AND inst.university's requirement with institution references expanded to their knowledge requirements. Institutional presence is not evaluable (no institutions system); ADR-029 §8. D-062 / ADR-043 (2026-10-22): the civic atom legal_code_roman is DROPPED from the stage — civics are funded by their own Civics Points, so a technology gate on a civic would couple the two lanes; inst.university still requires library AND legal_code_roman (the institution, not the stage, needs the civic).

technologies.name: Controlled-fire pyrotechnology
technologies.desc: Advanced, deliberate use of controlled fire — sustained managed hearths and earth ovens, heat treatment of stone, planned landscape burning. Fire itself (making, keeping, cooking) is baseline and needs no research (D-047 ruling 2).
technologies.emerged: ~164 kya heat-treated silcrete (Pinnacle Point); routine by ~70 kya

capabilities: heat treatment of stone and wood
techniques: Heat treatment of silcrete and flint

costRationale.note: founding technology of all pyrotechnology

technologies.name: Oldowan flaking
technologies.desc: Simple hard-hammer percussion producing choppers and sharp flakes.

technologies.name: Prepared-core (Levallois)
technologies.desc: Shaping a core so a flake of predetermined form detaches — standardised points.

technologies.name: Blade production
technologies.desc: Long parallel-sided blades struck from prismatic cores — efficient use of raw material, many tool forms from one core.
technologies.emerged: ~40 kya Upper Palaeolithic; earlier in Africa (~70 kya)

eurekas.text: An obsidian or fine flint source is in range
eurekas.justification: Blade industries cluster around high-quality obsidian and flint sources.

technologies.name: Pressure flaking
technologies.desc: Removing flakes by pressing rather than striking — fine, thin, symmetrical points.

costRationale.note: a skilled refinement of knapping

technologies.name: Heat treatment of stone
technologies.desc: Heating silcrete or chert to improve flaking — the first pyrotechnology applied to a material property.

capabilities: workable stone from poor raw material

technologies.name: Microliths and composite tools
technologies.desc: Small geometric blade segments set in series into wood or bone — replaceable cutting edges, barbed points.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) re-score: novelty 1.0 unchanged (typical: a new tool concept on known techniques); difficulty 0.0 unchanged (A1 prior); material 0.0 unchanged (local stone, wood, adhesive); institutional 0.0 unchanged (A1 prior); breadth 0.5 unchanged (sickle and composite arms downstream); prereq_complexity 0.0 -> 0.5 (two top-level requirements by the ledger convention). 260 -> 370 RP; the only change is the convention consequence of a causal edge.

technologies.name: Ground-edge axe
technologies.desc: Axes shaped by grinding rather than flaking — durable, resharpenable. Japan and Australia 25,000 years before the Neolithic.

technologies.name: Compound adhesives
technologies.desc: Engineered binders — resin loaded with ochre or beeswax, heat-processed bitumen — for load-bearing composite hafting. Simple gum, resin and sinew binding is baseline (D-047 ruling 3).

eurekas.text: Resin, bitumen or ochre is already gathered and worked for daily binding
eurekas.justification: Compound adhesives were refined where people already handled resin, bitumen and ochre every day (Sibudu ochre-loaded resin ~70 kya; Umm el Tlel bitumen): long familiarity with the raw binder under heat and mixing is what revealed the engineered recipe.

capabilities: load-bearing compound adhesive for composite hafting

technologies.name: Birch-bark tar
technologies.desc: Dry distillation of birch bark to produce tar — a manufactured adhesive requiring controlled heating without oxygen.

technologies.name: Composite hafting
technologies.desc: Precision-fitted composite tools — shaped tang, socket or split haft bound with sinew and compound adhesive — that survive repeated impact. Simple hafted tools are baseline (D-047 ruling 3).

technologies.name: Cordage
technologies.desc: Twisting plant or animal fibre into string and rope.
technologies.emerged: ~50 kya Abri du Maras (direct); older inferred

technologies.name: Basketry
technologies.desc: Woven or coiled containers from plant material — the container before pottery.
technologies.emerged: ~27 kya Pavlov impressions; ~10 kya Guitarrero Cave

technologies.name: Spear-thrower
technologies.desc: Lever that extends the throwing arm — darts at higher velocity and range.

technologies.name: Simple bow
technologies.desc: Self bow of a single stave with a fibre string — stored-energy projectile.

technologies.name: Sling
technologies.desc: Cord pouch launching stones — cheap, deadly, a shepherd's weapon.

technologies.name: Framed hut
technologies.desc: Durable dwelling on a frame — mammoth-bone, timber post, or turf — for seasonal occupation.

technologies.name: Hide working
technologies.desc: Scraping, stretching, and softening animal skins into usable leather and fur.

technologies.name: Eyed needle and sewing
technologies.desc: Bone needles for fitted, sewn garments — cold-climate expansion enabler.

technologies.name: Sea-crossing raft
technologies.desc: Large lashed log or reed rafts with steering oars, built for open-water crossings beyond sight of land. Simple riverine and shore-hugging craft are baseline (D-047 ruling 7); research unlocks the class and builds no vessel.

capabilities: open-water crossing beyond sight of land

technologies.name: Load-carrying dugout
technologies.desc: Large log hollowed by fire and adze into a stable load-carrying hull. Simple log floats and small canoes for river crossing are baseline (D-047 ruling 7); research unlocks the class and builds no vessel.

eurekas.text: Large trees grow beside navigable water
eurekas.justification: Dugouts need big straight trunks near rivers or lakes.

capabilities: lake and estuary freight by dugout

technologies.name: Line and pelagic fishing
technologies.desc: Specialised hook-and-line gear — shell or bone hooks, weighted lines, lures — for deep-water and pelagic species. Basic fishing is baseline and needs no hook or node (D-047 rulings 4 and 6).

eurekas.justification: Hooks appear among coastal and riverine foragers.

technologies.name: Grinding stone
technologies.desc: Quern and handstone for processing seeds, tubers, pigment.
technologies.emerged: ~30 kya Bilancino; routine in Natufian ~12 kya

technologies.name: Dog domestication
technologies.desc: First domesticate, from wolf, well before agriculture.

eurekas.justification: Dog domestication required sustained contact with wolf populations.

technologies.name: Pigment processing
technologies.desc: Grinding and mixing ochre for marking, adhesive additive, hide preservation.

technologies.name: Bone and antler tools
technologies.desc: Carved bone, antler, ivory — awls, points, harpoons, needles. Requires groove-and-splinter technique.

technologies.name: Oil lamp
technologies.desc: Stone lamp burning animal fat with a moss wick — light in caves.

technologies.name: Tally marks
technologies.desc: Incised counting marks on bone — Ishango, Lebombo.

technologies.name: Cereal cultivation
technologies.desc: Deliberate sowing of wild-type cereal — tending before genetic domestication. Pre-domestication cultivation lasted ~1,000 years.
technologies.emerged: ~11,500 BCE Levant (PPNA); independently by ~8,000 BCE in northern China (millet) and by ~7,000 BCE on the Yangtze (rice) and in Mesoamerica (maize)

eurekas.justification: Cultivation began where wild wheat, barley or rice were already harvested.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) re-score: novelty 1.0 - authored, unchanged | difficulty 0.5 - A2 prior, unchanged | material 0.0 (was 2.0) - material means material requirements (ledger 7.4): sowing and tending a wild grass needs no engineered material (sickle and quern are separate nodes); 2.0 is the loader maximum and exceeds tin_bronze (1.5), while the sibling crop nodes rice_wet, millet, sorghum_pearl_millet, root_crop, legume and flax all score 0.0 | institutional 0.25 - A2 prior, unchanged | breadth 1.5 - authored (farming yield switch, 12 dependants) | prereq_complexity 0.0 - one requirement. Content reason (peer consistency) only; not chosen for pacing (D-046 §1). Old 3,520 RP -> new 880 RP.

technologies.name: Wheat and barley domestication
technologies.desc: Non-shattering rachis, larger grain — the genetic result of ~1,000 years of harvesting with sickles.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) re-score: novelty 2.0 - authored (domestication syndrome) | difficulty 0.5 - A2 prior | material 0.0 (was 2.0) - the domestic plant is the outcome, not a material requirement; rice_wet, also novelty 2.0, scores 0.0 | institutional 0.25 - A2 prior | breadth 0.5 - authored | prereq_complexity 0.0 - one requirement. Old 3,520 RP -> new 880 RP.

technologies.name: Wet rice cultivation
technologies.desc: Paddy cultivation of domesticated rice — flooded fields, transplanting.

eurekas.text: Wild rice grows in wetlands in range
eurekas.justification: Rice was domesticated from wild rice in the Yangtze wetlands.

capabilities: highest yield per area of any pre-modern cereal

technologies.name: Millet cultivation
technologies.desc: Broomcorn and foxtail millet — dry-farming cereal of the Yellow River.

eurekas.justification: Foxtail and broomcorn millet were domesticated from wild grasses in northern China.

technologies.name: Maize domestication
technologies.desc: From teosinte — the most genetically transformed of all crops; took millennia to become a staple.

eurekas.justification: Maize was domesticated from teosinte in the Balsas valley.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) re-score: novelty 2.0 - authored (most transformed crop) | difficulty 0.5 - A2 prior, authored (the protracted domestication is noted, not re-scored) | material 0.0 (was 2.0) - no material requirement beyond its siblings, which score 0.0 | institutional 0.25 - A2 prior | breadth 1.0 - authored | prereq_complexity 0.0 - one requirement. Old 4,970 RP -> new 1,240 RP.

technologies.name: African cereal domestication
technologies.desc: Sorghum and pearl millet — Sahel domesticates adapted to drought.

technologies.name: Root and tuber cultivation
technologies.desc: Vegetative propagation — taro, yam, potato, manioc, sweet potato. Different from seed agriculture: clonal, no seed to store.

capabilities: no granary needed — stored in ground

technologies.name: Legume cultivation
technologies.desc: Lentil, pea, chickpea, bean — protein and nitrogen fixation. Co-domesticated with cereals in every centre.

technologies.name: Fruit tree cultivation
technologies.desc: Olive, fig, date, grape — long-lived perennials requiring multi-decade investment and sedentism.

technologies.name: Sickle
technologies.desc: Curved harvesting blade — first microlith-set, then flint, then metal.

technologies.name: Hoe
technologies.desc: Hafted blade for tillage — the cultivation tool before the plough. Digging-stick cultivation is baseline (D-047).

technologies.name: Nixtamalization
technologies.desc: Cooking maize in alkaline solution — releases niacin, prevents pellagra. Maize as a staple depends on it.

eurekas.text: Wood ash or lime is used in cooking
eurekas.justification: Alkaline processing of maize used ash or lime.

capabilities: maize as sole staple without deficiency

costRationale.note: alkaline cooking with ash or lime; no engineered material

technologies.name: Sheep and goat domestication
technologies.desc: First herd animals — meat, later milk and wool.

eurekas.text: Wild sheep or goats range nearby
eurekas.justification: Mouflon and bezoar were domesticated in the Zagros and Taurus.

technologies.name: Cattle domestication
technologies.desc: Taurine (Near East) and zebu (Indus) — independently. Meat, then milk, traction, dung.
technologies.emerged: ~8,500 BCE Near East; ~7,000 BCE Indus; possibly Sahara

eurekas.justification: Cattle descend from aurochs domesticated in the Near East and South Asia.

technologies.name: Pig domestication
technologies.desc: From wild boar — independently in Near East and China. Omnivore; village scavenger.

eurekas.justification: Pigs were domesticated independently from wild boar in Anatolia and China.

technologies.name: Milking and dairying
technologies.desc: Exploiting living animals for milk — requires either lactase persistence or processing into cheese/yogurt.

technologies.name: Wool sheep and fleece
technologies.desc: Selection for fleece-bearing sheep — wool as a fibre.

technologies.name: Animal traction
technologies.desc: Yoking cattle to pull — the prerequisite for plough and cart.

technologies.name: Open-fired pottery
technologies.desc: Coil-built vessels fired in a bonfire — low temperature, porous, but a container that boils.
technologies.emerged: ~18,000 BCE Xianrendong; ~14,000 BCE Jomon; ~9,000 BCE Near East; ~9,400 BCE Mali

technologies.name: Updraft kiln
technologies.desc: Enclosed firing chamber with a firebox below — >900°C, controlled atmosphere. The thermal precondition for smelting.

technologies.name: Fast wheel (throwing)
technologies.desc: Flywheel-momentum wheel permitting thrown pottery — mass production, a specialist craft.

technologies.name: Mudbrick
technologies.desc: Sun-dried clay bricks — modular, repairable, multi-storey.

technologies.name: Lime plaster
technologies.desc: Burning limestone to quicklime, slaking, applying — floors, walls, and the first chemically transformed building material.
technologies.emerged: ~10,000 BCE late Natufian Levant (Nahal Ein Gev II burial plaster); ~8,000 BCE PPNB floors and statues (Ain Ghazal, Yiftahel)

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) re-score: novelty 1.0 unchanged (first chemically transformed building material) · difficulty 0.5 unchanged (A2 prior) · material 1.5 unchanged (limestone burnt and slaked) · institutional 0.25 unchanged (A2 prior) · breadth 0.5 unchanged (floors, walls, statuary; one dependant) · prereq_complexity 0.5 -> 0.0 (one requirement). Cost 1,760 -> 1,240.

technologies.name: Timber-frame construction
technologies.desc: Post-and-beam structures — longhouses of the LBK, pile dwellings.

technologies.name: Dry-stone construction
technologies.desc: Walls and structures of fitted unmortared stone.
technologies.emerged: ~10,000 BCE Göbekli Tepe; ~3,000 BCE Skara Brae

technologies.name: Dug well
technologies.desc: Excavated shaft to groundwater — settlement independent of surface water.
technologies.emerged: ~8,000 BCE Atlit-Yam (stone-lined); ~5,200 BCE LBK oak-lined wells (Saxony)

technologies.name: Grain fermentation (beer)
technologies.desc: Malting and brewing — grain into a storable, nutritious, safe drink.
technologies.prereq: (cereal_domesticated OR rice_wet OR millet OR maize OR sorghum_pearl_millet) AND pottery_open_fired

technologies.name: Wine and fruit fermentation
technologies.desc: Fermenting grape, honey, fruit.

technologies.name: Oil pressing
technologies.desc: Extracting olive, sesame, flax oil by crushing and pressing.

technologies.name: Salt production
technologies.desc: Evaporating brine or mining rock salt — the preservative and the trade good.

eurekas.text: Brine springs, salt pans or a sea coast
eurekas.justification: Salt making follows natural brine and evaporation sites.

technologies.name: Flax cultivation
technologies.desc: Growing flax for linen fibre and oil.
technologies.emerged: ~8,000 BCE Levant (wild flax use ~30 kya Dzudzuana)

technologies.name: Spindle spinning
technologies.desc: Drop spindle with whorl — continuous thread from fibre.
technologies.prereq: cordage AND (flax OR wool OR cotton_cultivation)

technologies.name: Warp-weighted loom
technologies.desc: Vertical loom with weighted warps — wide cloth, complex weaves.

technologies.name: Dyeing
technologies.desc: Colouring fibre with plant and mineral dyes — madder, woad, indigo, with mordants.

technologies.name: Native copper working
technologies.desc: Cold-hammering and annealing metallic copper nuggets — beads, awls. Not smelting.

technologies.name: Copper smelting
technologies.desc: Reducing malachite/azurite to metal in a charcoal fire — the first extractive metallurgy.

eurekas.justification: Smelting followed working native copper and ore-bearing malachite.

technologies.name: Charcoal making
technologies.desc: Pyrolysing wood in a covered pile — a fuel hot enough for metallurgy.

technologies.name: Open-mould casting
technologies.desc: Pouring molten copper into a one-piece stone mould — axes, blades.

technologies.name: Native gold and silver
technologies.desc: Working native gold and silver — ornament, then value store.

technologies.name: Basin irrigation
technologies.desc: Trapping floodwater in bunded basins — Nile and Indus mode.

technologies.name: Canal irrigation
technologies.desc: Diverting river water through dug channels — Mesopotamian mode. Requires levelling and maintenance.

eurekas.text: An arid floodplain watered by a river
eurekas.justification: Canal irrigation arose on the Tigris–Euphrates, Nile and Indus floodplains.

technologies.name: Agricultural terracing
technologies.desc: Stepped fields on slopes — soil retention, water control, arable from hillside.

eurekas.justification: Terracing answers hillside farming (Andes, Levant, southern China).

technologies.name: Sledge
technologies.desc: Runners for hauling loads over snow, mud, or grass — the vehicle before the wheel.

technologies.name: Solid wheel and axle
technologies.desc: Disc wheel on a fixed or rotating axle — from the potter's wheel principle to the vehicle.

technologies.name: Ox cart
technologies.desc: Two-wheeled cart drawn by oxen — bulk haulage overland.

capabilities: bulk overland transport at cart range

technologies.name: Trackway
technologies.desc: Trackway — an IMPROVED PATH, not an engineered road: timber causeway and corduroy across marsh, cleared and stoned track (Sweet Track). An infrastructure-class unlock (path tier): road development builds the trackways, and basic dirt paths are baseline (D-047 ruling 8; ADR-032). The engineered built road additionally needs dry-stone construction (infra.road_built requires track_road AND stone_dry).

capabilities: trackway infrastructure class (path tier: timber causeway and stoned track)

technologies.name: Ard plough
technologies.desc: Animal-drawn scratch plough — multiplies cultivable area per farmer.
technologies.emerged: ~4,000 BCE (plough marks under barrows; Uruk pictograph)

technologies.name: Clay tokens
technologies.desc: Geometric clay counters for commodities — one token per unit.

technologies.name: Stamp seal
technologies.desc: Carved stone impressed in clay — ownership, authentication.

technologies.name: Lunar calendar
technologies.desc: Tracking months by moon phases — sowing and festival timing.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) re-score: novelty 1.0 (unchanged): reckoning time by lunations is a new concept but not paradigm-founding · difficulty 0.5 (unchanged): A2 prior; counting phases extends tally practice · material 0 (unchanged): no apparatus is needed · institutional 3.0 → 0.25: A2 prior; the evidence is a hunter-gatherer monument, and no institution is required · breadth 1.0 (unchanged): seasonal and ritual timing, plus the base of calendar_civil, the non-Babylonian astronomy_records route and latitude_sailing · prereq_complexity 0 (unchanged): one prerequisite. The reason is the institutional score, not pacing (D-046 §1). The earlier completion it causes is a consequence, not the aim.

technologies.name: Trepanation
technologies.desc: Surgical opening of the skull — with survival rates over 50%.
technologies.emerged: ~5,000 BCE Ensisheim (Alsace); argued earlier ~7,300–6,200 BCE Vasilyevka II (Ukraine); widespread Neolithic

costRationale.note: skilled stone-tool surgery

technologies.name: Arsenical bronze
technologies.desc: Copper smelted from arsenic-bearing ores — harder than copper, castable, and NEEDS NO TIN. Most early "bronze" was this.

eurekas.text: Arsenic-bearing copper ores (fahlore, enargite, arsenopyrite-rich deposits) are smelted locally
eurekas.justification: Arsenical copper arose where smelters worked arsenic-rich ores (Caucasus, Anatolia, Iran) and met its harder, castable metal and garlic-smelling fumes. Generic copper-ore stock carries no arsenic signal, so the condition reads arsenical ore specifically; no goods or resource state distinguishes it yet.

capabilities: harder tools and weapons without tin trade

technologies.name: Tin bronze
technologies.desc: Copper alloyed with ~10% tin — superior, reproducible, but tin sources are rare and distant.

eurekas.text: Tin ore is held, locally or by trade
eurekas.justification: Tin bronze depended on access to rare tin sources, often by long-distance exchange.

technologies.name: Two-piece and closed-mould casting
technologies.desc: Bivalve moulds for symmetrical objects — socketed axes, spearheads.

technologies.name: Lost-wax casting
technologies.desc: Wax model, clay investment, wax melted out, metal poured — any shape, one use.
technologies.emerged: ~4,000 BCE Mehrgarh (unalloyed copper amulet); ~3,700 BCE Nahal Mishmar; Indus ~2,500 BCE

technologies.name: Sheet metalwork
technologies.desc: Hammering bronze into sheet — vessels, helmets, armour by raising and chasing.

technologies.name: Shaft mining
technologies.desc: Vertical shafts and galleries following ore — Grimes Graves flint, Timna copper, Great Orme.

technologies.name: Proto-cuneiform
technologies.desc: Pictographic accounting tablets — commodity + number, no syntax.

technologies.name: Cuneiform (full writing)
technologies.desc: Phonetic signs, syntax — language on clay. Sumerian, then Akkadian, Hittite, Elamite.

technologies.name: Egyptian hieroglyphic
technologies.desc: Logo-consonantal script — independent or stimulus-diffused from Mesopotamia (debated).

technologies.name: Oracle bone script
technologies.desc: Earliest Chinese writing — divination records, ancestor of all later Chinese script.

technologies.name: Papyrus
technologies.desc: Writing surface from pith strips — light, portable, and the first document technology.

technologies.name: Sexagesimal place-value
technologies.desc: Base-60 positional notation — the first place-value system.

technologies.name: Babylonian arithmetic
technologies.desc: Reciprocal tables, squares, quadratic problems — computational mathematics.

technologies.name: Land surveying
technologies.desc: Measuring and recording field boundaries — rope-stretchers, the 3-4-5 triangle.

technologies.name: Motor road (highway)
technologies.desc: Graded, surfaced, grade-separated road for motor traffic — Milano–Laghi autostrada 1924, Cologne–Bonn 1932, Reichsautobahn and US Interstate. An infrastructure-class unlock (highway tier): road development builds the highways as new alignments beside the older roads (ADR-032).

capabilities: highway infrastructure class: motor road, the bulk road-freight corridor

costRationale.note: ADR-029 methodology: U x K^magnitude = 92.4 x 2^8.5 = 33,449 -> 33,450. Novelty 0.5 (a road class, derivative of the automobile and engineered roads); difficulty 2.5 (grade separation, engineered alignments); material 1.5 (reinforced concrete / bitumen surfaces); institutional 2.5 (state highway authorities and national programmes); breadth 0.5; prerequisite complexity 1.0 (three AND prerequisites across engineering and natural science).

technologies.name: Trade
technologies.desc: Formal exchange between communities: goods valued against a counted standard and carried by pack animal or boat to partners beyond the settlement — the caravan and boat trade of the Uruk expansion and the Old Assyrian merchants of Kanesh. Within-settlement sharing and exchange need no research; trade BETWEEN settlements (domestic or foreign) does. Placement: Civ VI unlocks trade routes and the Trader with the Ancient-Era Foreign Trade civic (after Code of Laws); here the causal prerequisites are a record of quantity (clay tokens) and a carrier for goods over distance (donkey, camel or the square sail).
technologies.emerged: ~3,500 BCE Uruk-expansion exchange network; ~1,900 BCE Old Assyrian donkey-caravan trade (Kanesh)
technologies.prereq: token_counting AND (donkey OR camel OR sail_square)

techniques: Pack-animal and boat haulage of goods for exchange

costRationale.note: R2a: the Trade capability (Director decision 1/13). Priced on the existing banded model as a T2 organisational node one tier above its counting prerequisite; same magnitude as arithmetic_babylonian.

technologies.name: Cotton cultivation
technologies.desc: Growing cotton as a fibre crop, domesticated independently in South Asia, Africa and the Americas — a second great plant fibre beside flax and wool.
technologies.emerged: ~5,500 BCE Mehrgarh (Indus, cotton fibres); ~4,000 BCE coastal Peru (Huaca Prieta textiles); four species domesticated independently

eurekas.justification: The same wild-progenitor circumstance as flax, millet and maize: domestication began where wild Gossypium grew.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0 - a new crop, typical | difficulty 0.5 - A2 prior | material 0.0 - no engineered material, as for its crop siblings | institutional 0.25 - A2 prior | breadth 0.5 - one fibre capability (spinning, ginning) | prereq_complexity 0.0 - one OR group. Magnitude 2.25 -> 440 RP.

technologies.name: Ashlar (dressed-stone) masonry
technologies.desc: Cutting and dressing stone blocks to fit tightly — the masonry of pyramids, temples, towers and stone arches.
technologies.emerged: ~2,650 BCE Egypt (Djoser's step pyramid, Saqqara); ~600 BCE Greek temples; ~1,450 CE Inca Andes (independent)

capabilities: stone voussoirs for arches, bridges and vaults

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0: a typical advance on dry stone (true faces, coursing) · difficulty 1.0: A3 prior · material 0.75: copper chisels and abrasive saws, quarrying · institutional 0.75: A3 prior (state works crews) · breadth 1.0: fortification, dressed-stone bridges and vaults, lighthouse · prereq_complexity 0.5: two requirements. Magnitude 5.0 -> 2,960 RP.

technologies.name: Silver refining by cupellation
technologies.desc: Separating silver from lead by burning the lead away in a hot hearth; the same fire assay tests gold and silver.
technologies.emerged: ~3,600 BCE Tepe Sialk (Iran); ~3,300 BCE Habuba Kabira (Syria) and Fatmali-Kalecik (Anatolia) - litharge from cupellation

eurekas.text: Argentiferous lead ore (galena) is smelted locally
eurekas.justification: Cupellation arose where silver-bearing lead ores were worked (eastern Anatolia, northern Syria, the Iranian plateau; later Laurion). No goods or resource state distinguishes argentiferous ore yet.

capabilities: silver separated from argentiferous lead by oxidizing the lead to litharge
fire assay of gold and silver (cupellation at small scale)

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0 (a new refining principle - oxidizing the base metal away - built on smelting; typical, not paradigm-founding); difficulty 1.0 (A3 prior; about 1,000 C with an air blast, within Chalcolithic furnaces); material 0.75 (argentiferous lead ore, bone-ash or marl cupels, a blown hearth; as copper smelting); institutional 0.75 (A3 prior; specialist metalworkers, palace and temple demand); breadth 0.5 (silver supply for weighed-silver exchange and later coinage; fire assay); prereq_complexity 0.5 (two top-level requirements). Magnitude 4.5 -> 2,090 RP, the same profile as wheel_spoked (A3).

technologies.name: Mesoamerican writing
technologies.desc: Full writing grown out of calendar notation — the dated monuments and bark-paper books of the Zapotec and Maya.
technologies.emerged: ~650 BCE calendar notation (San Andres, Tabasco); ~600-500 BCE Zapotec (San Jose Mogote); ~300 BCE Maya (San Bartolo)

capabilities: full writing grown from calendrical notation

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 2.0: an independent invention of full writing (as cuneiform, hieroglyphic, chinese_script); difficulty 1.0 and institutional 0.75: A3 prior (court scribes of early states); material 0.0: stone, stucco, bark paper and ceramics need no new material; breadth 1.5: the same downstream scope as its peers once it joins the generic-writing OR groups (D03's surveying, geometry_practical, calendar_civil, astronomy_records; entity OR groups requested); prereq_complexity 0.0: one requirement. 5.25 = 3,520 RP, equal to hieroglyphic: not a cheaper route - its closure (via calendar_lunar, 4,180 RP) costs more than chinese_script's.

technologies.name: Ore prospecting
technologies.desc: Reading the land for ore: coloured stains, weathered outcrops and stream placers that betray copper and tin.
technologies.emerged: ~5,000 BCE (copper-ore veins located and worked at Rudna Glava, Vinca culture); ~3,000 BCE (cassiterite worked at Kestel-Goltepe, Taurus; debated)

capabilities: surface indications of ore (colour stains, gossans) and placer working

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: A3 prior (difficulty 1.0, institutional 0.75); novelty 1.0 (a practice, not a paradigm); material 0.0 (picks and washing pans); breadth 1.0 (identifies tin ore, a good today, and silver-bearing galena with cupellation; trial assay for proving; root of mineralogy; prerequisite of tin_bronze if D02 adopts the edge); prereq_complexity 0.0 (one requirement). Magnitude 3.75 -> 1,240 RP.

root extraction and elimination for simultaneous linear problems (Nine Chapters methods)

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 2.0: an independent decimal place-value calculating system (with a blank for zero and signed red/black rods), the same paradigm score as numeral_sexagesimal and hindu_arabic · difficulty 1.5: A5 prior · material 0: bamboo or bone rods · institutional 1.25: A5 prior; state scribes and calendar officials · breadth 0.5: one OR dependant (algebra) plus the board algorithms of the Nine Chapters · prereq_complexity 0: one prerequisite. costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0: a typical advance (pattern storage in the harness) · difficulty 1.5: A5 prior · material 0.75: multi-heddle harness, silk warps · institutional 1.25: A5 prior (state and royal silk workshops of Shu) · breadth 0.0: one dependant (jacquard) · prereq_complexity 0.5: two requirements. capabilities: stone-throwing artillery by lever and sling (crew-hauled)

capabilities: cased boreholes hundreds of metres deep for brine and natural gas
drilled wells reach fluids no shaft can (later petroleum)

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0 (a new extraction method distinct from digging; typical); difficulty 1.75 (A6 prior; heavy bits, casings, recovering stuck tools); material 0.75 (iron bits, bamboo or timber derricks, casings and cables); institutional 1.25 (A6 prior; the Sichuan salt industry's capital and specialist crews); breadth 0.5 (brine and gas wells; petroleum wells and prospecting boreholes through adopting lanes); prereq_complexity 0.5 (two top-level requirements). technologies.name: Rifled barrel
technologies.desc: Spiral grooves in the barrel spin the bullet for accurate aimed fire at long range.

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0: a new principle (spin-stabilised projectile) applied to an existing weapon. difficulty 2.0: A7 prior (cutting even helical grooves on a rifling bench). material 0.0: ordinary gun barrels. institutional 1.5: A7 prior (gunsmith craft). breadth 1.0: the whole rifled-weapon line (rifles, rifled artillery) plus a light-infantry identity. prereq_complexity 0.0: one prerequisite. technologies.name: Systematic mineralogy

technologies.emerged: 1546 CE (Agricola, De natura fossilium); 1758 CE (Cronstedt's blowpipe mineral analysis)

capabilities: typing of unfamiliar mineral occurrences in observed land (physical properties, blowpipe and wet tests)

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: A7 prior (2.0/1.5); novelty 1.0 (systematisation of observation, not a new paradigm); material 0.75 (blowpipe kits, reagents, glassware); breadth 1.0 (identification of unfamiliar ores; root of stratigraphy); prereq_complexity 0.5 (two requirements). technologies.name: Probability and statistics

technologies.emerged: 1654-1812 CE (Pascal and Fermat 1654; Bernoulli's law of large numbers 1713; Laplace 1812)

capabilities: statistical analysis of counts and errors

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 2.0: paradigm - a mathematics of chance and inference | difficulty 2.0: A7 prior | material 0.0: mathematics | institutional 1.5: A7 prior - academies and correspondence networks | breadth 1.0: statistical genetics, epidemiology, insurance, statistical mechanics, machine learning | prereq_complexity 0.0: one requirement. technologies.name: Biological classification
technologies.desc: Naming and classifying living species in one orderly system.

eurekas.text: Ocean voyaging returns specimens from distant regions
eurekas.justification: Specimens from long voyages - and Linnaeus's travelling students - supplied the material systematic classification organised; ocean-going ships are the knowledge state that makes such voyages possible. Not implied: taxonomy requires only printing_press.

capabilities: systematic naming and classification of species

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0: a systematic method for an existing practice of natural history | difficulty 2.0: A7 prior | material 0.0: no apparatus beyond herbaria | institutional 1.5: A7 prior - botanical gardens, herbaria, academies | breadth 0.5: feeds evolution and systematic botany | prereq_complexity 0.0: one requirement. Same magnitude as selective_breeding (5.0).

technologies.name: Breech-loading rifle
technologies.desc: Rifles loaded at the breech with cartridges, so soldiers can fire rapidly from cover.
technologies.emerged: 1841 CE Dreyse needle gun (Prussia); metallic-cartridge and bolt-action rifles from the 1860s
technologies.prereq: rifling AND flintlock AND chemistry_quantitative AND interchangeable_parts

eurekas.text: A rival's breech-loader-armed infantry has been met in battle
eurekas.justification: The needle gun was decisive at Königgrätz (1866); the Chassepot, a needle-gun derivative, entered French service that year, and Germany's Mauser followed in 1871 — war exposure accelerated breech-loader adoption (RESEARCHED).

costRationale.note: ADR-045 (D-062) new node: novelty 1.0: a new firearm class (a self-contained primed cartridge loaded at the breech). difficulty 2.5: A8 prior (gas-tight breech). material 0.0: firearm-family convention (matchlock, wheellock, flintlock 0.0); the metals come from its prerequisites. institutional 2.0: A8 prior (state arsenals). breadth 1.0: rifle infantry, marksmen and carbine cavalry identities plus the machine gun. prereq_complexity 1.0: four conjuncts. Magnitude 7.5 -> 16,730 RP.

technologies.name: Machine gun
technologies.desc: Weapons that keep firing while the trigger is held.

Magnitude 6.0 -> 5,910 RP.

civics.name: Taxation
civics.desc: Taxation: the levy of tribute in kind — a counted share of the harvest, herd or craft output owed to the ruler or temple, assessed against the harvest and delivered into sealed stores. Its evidence is the Uruk and Ur III grain-receipt tablets, the sealed storerooms of the Ubaid and Uruk temples, and the Egyptian harvest assessment recorded beside the Nile gauge. A community without a record of what is owed has gifts and feasting, not a levy, so no Stone Age society taxes. Researching it gives the polity the knowledge of the tax edict (SetTaxRate); the edict is operational only once the polity has entered Age III, the Bronze Age (sim.json governance.taxationMinAge). Related refinements, which no longer gate the edict: tax assessment by computation (arithmetic_babylonian), taxation by area (surveying), by weight (standard_weights) and in coin (coinage_electrum). Placement: Civ VI has no tax technology — governments and their policies come through civics, starting with the first civic, Code of Laws (Chiefdom); here the causal prerequisites are counted obligations (clay tokens), sealed stores under administrative control (stamp seal) and an administrative record beyond memory (proto-cuneiform, hieroglyphic or Chinese script).
